🔍 Hack attacks, digital disruptions are ‘new normal’ – former NSA chief
The wave of high-profile digital outages and [cyberattacks](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78097) rocking companies, banks, the FAA, and even [the FBI and NSA](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78036) are only the start, with AI tools’ ability to uncover vulnerabilities, and aging infrastructure designed to handle less complex threats characterized as a toxic combination.
🔊“What we are seeing is a new normal,” ex-NSA and US Cyber Command chief Paul Nakasone said at a conference this week.
“Industries and agencies are trying to rapidly modernize, and at the same time, defend themselves” against “the most disruptive technology” in history, Nakasone, who now sits on the board of OpenAI – one of the tech giants making such attacks possible, explained.
Big Tech blames aging hardware and software for the spike in issues, with Google head of global risk Jeanette Manfra telling WaPo “critical systems are deeply interconnected, and many still rely on brittle legacy architectures where a single vendor misconfiguration, hardware failure or cyberattack can trigger cascading failures.”
Cybersecurity experts told the paper there’s enough “technical debt” in global systems to spend up to 18 months fixing, and that companies and governments face “a Y2K-level of effort in terms of getting our infrastructure up to speed.”
🗣“The only challenge with that is, if the models keep getting more and more capable, I don’t know what that means,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has said.
Officials insist the spike in incidents is not connected, blaming them on [foreign actors or](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77557) lone wolf attackers, even though they line up perfectly with former Google and DoD [AI scientist Nate](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74844) Soares’ blueprint for how independent-minded machines could try to replicate themselves and secure access to resources.
Others fear the rise in cybersecurity incidents [blamed on AI](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78121) may be hiding something more sinister: a justification to eliminate online anonymity, [restrictions on open-source AI tools](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76882), an expansion of AI-based surveillance and automated censorship, or even a splintering of the global internet.

events.text:
🤥 Trump keeps trying to reach out to Kim and keeps getting ghosted – report
 
The Trump administration’s efforts to restart dialogue with Kim Jong Un have gone nowhere, according to WSJ.
🔴 The White House tried to arrange a meeting on the sidelines of the US president’s Asia tour, but North Korea set conditions that Trump refused to accept
🔴 Trump had earlier tried to call Kim, but to no avail
🔴 He then wrote a letter and sent a courier to the North Korean mission to the UN in New York. The North Korean side, however, returned it unopened
The biggest stumbling block in the negotiations is the denuclearization question. The US floated the idea of offering a formal declaration putting an end to the Korean War and issuing a statement that would soften the demand for complete denuclearization—in return for limits on nuclear and missile testing.
👉 North Korea, for its part, wants to be recognized as an official nuclear power. And its arsenal has ballooned in the meantime—from roughly 30 warheads to 60—with solid-fuel ICBMs capable of reaching the US mainland already deployed. On top of that, Pyongyang keeps deepening its military partnership with Russia, beefing up its weaponry with hypersonic technology, reconnaissance satellites, underwater drones, and next-generation missiles.
Previous Trump-Kim talks collapsed in 2019 after the North Korean leader offered to close some nuclear facilities in exchange for sanctions relief, while the US pressed for a freeze on all nuclear and missile programs, to be followed by a roadmap to full denuclearization. Trump walked away abruptly without a deal—and North Korea promptly resumed short-range ballistic missile tests.
Then the pandemic shut the door on diplomacy in 2020, and the Biden administration gave North Korea low priority. Talks have now been revived, but they’ve yet to produce anything close to a breakthrough—and the US appears to have no leverage left over from the old Trump-Kim “friendship.”

🇮🇱 Israeli spy links shadow Trump's pick for top US cyber post – report
President Trump's pick for the White House national cyber director, Kirsten Davies, has extensive business connections to Israeli cybersecurity firms founded by former intelligence officials, an investigation by ¡DoNotPanic! reveals.
Davies’ financial disclosures show that she served on the boards of three companies linked to veterans of Israel's Unit 8200 while building her career in the private cybersecurity sector.
Key connections include:
♦️ Team8: Davies spent nearly a decade on the board of the venture capital firm founded by Nadav Zafrir, a former commander of Unit 8200 who later became head of Israel's military Cyber Command.
♦️ Talon Cyber Security: She also served on the board of the Israeli startup founded by former Unit 8200 personnel Ohad Bobrov and Ofer Ben-Noon.
♦️ Claroty: In 2023, Davies joined the company's advisory board. Founded by former Unit 8200 commander Amir Zilberstein, Claroty subsequently secured contracts to protect sensitive US military and intelligence facilities, including missile sites, shortly before Davies joined the Pentagon as its chief information officer.
Davies also reportedly served on the board of US investment firm NightDragon, which has invested in more than 25 Israeli cybersecurity companies founded by former intelligence personnel.
Earlier this week, Trump tapped Davies touted by the White House as "a battle-tested cyber leader," to lead the Office of the National Cyber Director in the aftermath of a wave of outages affecting American big tech companies, banks, airlines, and [federal agencies.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78078)

🇺🇸✈️Second US jet declares mid-air emergency amid escalating shadow war in the Gulf
 
A US F-35A jet transmitted transponder squawk code 7700 (in-flight emergency) over the eastern UAE early Sunday morning, with OSINT observers tracking the jet’s diversion to Dhafra Air Base in Abu Dhabi.
The code was issued after the jet was tracked flying in the vicinity of Hormuz.
7700 is the universal aviation code for a general emergency, and is sent out to report mechanical issues, medical emergencies, fuel problems, and in the case of military aircraft, potential battle damage.
The F-35A was the second US warplane to squawk the code in 48 hours, with an [F-16](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78131) doing so late Friday. Iran’s military subsequently released footage of the jet’s narrow escape from a SAM exploding directly behind it. CENTCOM says the incident never happened.
Iranian officials, the military and IRGC have yet to comment on the F-35A’s distress call. CENTCOM is also silent.
Iran became the first nation to damage an [F-35 jet](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/67820) in combat in March, and reported the destruction of three F-35s on the ground at a base [in Jordan in July](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72888) (the US has denied those claims).
The distress calls come amid [a broader regional escalation](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78153), including Iranian attacks on US bases and the destruction of multimillion-dollar [drones over Hormuz](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78154), amid reports that Israel is again lobbying President Trump to resume a full-scale war.
